content.summary_of_the_paper:
In their work, the authors prove a rigorous bound on the generalization gap of machine learning models in terms of the sample complexity and the mutual information (MI) between the input data and the intermediate layer activations (the information bottleneck). The new bound improves over previous work by moving the exponential growth in the MI to a linear one. Since this bound is based on the assumption that intermediate layer activations that are independent from the data distribution, it can fail to capture models that are trained. Addressing this limitation, the authors give a second bound which takes into account the mutual information between the training data and the learned weights, which can be seen as a measurement of overfitting. This allows them to explicitly model the trade-off between minimising the information bottleneck (representational compression) and fitting the model to the training data.
In experimental results they show that both of these measurements together work better to capture the generalization error of a trained model rather than one of the measurements individually.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strong points:

- The results from the paper are interesting and important because they make the trade-off between overfitting to the data and finding a compressed representation to the generalised clear, that were not captured in similar models previously.
- The importance of this finding is stressed in that it both fixes the failure mode of a previous bound and the trade-off it exhibits is exhibited in practical experiments.
- The paper is very well written and concise, it strikes a good balance between detailing the results and putting them into context, making the results very accessible to readers.

Weak points:
- The experimental section compares several generalization estimators in terms of different MI measurements. It would be interesting to see how other metrics that estimate generalization perform too, just to put the importance of both overfitting estimator and the representational compression into a broader context.

Questions/ Additional Feedback:
- It would be helpful to be guided to some references, when the authors refer to other “existing bounds” at the end of Section 1, page 2.
- While the authors clearly make an effort to separate their work from a related line of work on the information bottleneck which sees it as an underlying mechanism of trained machine learning models rather than investigating its impact as a regulariser, it might be helpful give a half-sentence to the reader in the introduction already on how such a regulariser can practically be implemented and how computationally heavy it is.

Details
- on page 3, after eq(9), it seems that the definition of c_l^y is missing
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
While not checked in detail, the appendix of the paper seems to provide many more details with regards to the experiments which should make it easier to reproduce them.

The language and notation are complex but nonetheless clear enough and concise.

The work seems original and novel to me in the context of the literature it is presented in. Given my lack of detailed knowledge of the broader context this assessment relies largely on the authors presentation and references, and I cannot assess whether relevant related work was missed. I am also not confident enough in my knowledge of the field to access the novelty of the proof technique.

content.title: Response to Reviewer r4UJ
content.comment:
Thank you for the positive feedback and remarking that “the results from the paper are interesting and important” and “the paper is very well written and concise, it strikes a good balance between detailing the results and putting them into context, making the results very accessible to readers.” 

Your summary of the paper and comments are the most accurate and we appreciate your effort on this. Also, we highly appreciate the reviewer’s suggestions for further improvements, as they allowed us to improve the paper. Thank you! We revised the paper according to all of your suggestions as described below.

---
---

**Reviewer’s Comment**: “The experimental section compares several generalization estimators in terms of different MI measurements. It would be interesting to see how other metrics that estimate generalization perform too, just to put the importance of both overfitting estimator and the representational compression into a broader context.”

**Response**: We have added new results in tables 1 and 5 for other metrics associated with generalization: m log m where m is the number of parameters (i.e., the key factor in the VC dimension for neural networks [1-2]), and the sum and product of weight norms (i.e., the key factor in the Rademacher complexity for neural networks [3-4]). Empirically we found that metrics based on MI significantly outperformed these additional metrics in terms of correlations. 

This is partially because other metrics are designed for theoretical guarantees of PAC-learnability, uniform learnability, and nonuniform learnability while MI is designed for better correlations in practice by relaxing these guarantees. Thus, different metrics have different scopes and purposes. For example, if we want the guarantee of PAC-learnability, then we cannot use metrics based on MI and should use other metrics. If we want better correlations in practice without the PAC-learnability guarantee, then we can consider using metrics based on MI. In this sense, we cannot claim which metrics are better as it depends on what we want.

[1] Vladimir Vapnik. The nature of statistical learning theory. Springer science & business media,
1999.

[2] Shai Shalev-Shwartz and Shai Ben-David. Understanding machine learning: From theory to algorithms. Cambridge university press, 2014. 

[3] Peter L Bartlett and Shahar Mendelson. Rademacher and gaussian complexities: Risk bounds and structural results. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 3(Nov):463–482, 2002.

[4] Golowich Noah, Alexander Rakhlin, and Ohad Shamir. Size-independent sample complexity of neural networks. Conference On Learning Theory. PMLR, 2018.


---
---

**Reviewer’s Comment**: “It would be helpful to be guided to some references, when the authors refer to other “existing bounds” at the end of Section 1, page 2.”

**Response**: We added the new references by directly following your comment.

---
---

**Reviewer’s Comment**: “While the authors clearly make an effort to separate their work from a related line of work on the information bottleneck which sees it as an underlying mechanism of trained machine learning models rather than investigating its impact as a regulariser, it might be helpful give a half-sentence to the reader in the introduction already on how such a regulariser can practically be implemented and how computationally heavy it is.” 

**Response**: Based on your comment, we have added a note on the practical implementation in the introduction, and also updated appendix C and added fig. 4.  Below we give additional explanation. 

We implemented regularization of MI(X; Z) for the stochastic feature networks using the reparameterization trick and dual gradient descent, which is relatively straightforward and lightweight to use. In the forward pass, the neural network deterministically infers mean and variance of the latent feature distribution conditioned on each input, which defines the distribution P(Z | x) used in the MI(X; Z) formula. The expectation over P(x) and P(Z | x) in MI(X; Z), where P(Z | x) depends on neural network parameters, is rewritten as an expectation over P(x) and P(Q) where P(Q) is a fixed distribution over Gaussian noise that does not depend on the neural network parameters and Z is deterministically computed given Q and inferred mean an variance. This allows the neural network to be optimized with the objective L + lambda * (rho - MI(Z; X)), where L is the classification loss and lambda is a weighting coefficient and MI is approximated by Monte Carlo averaging, by averaging samples of the inner term of MI(Z; X), log (P(Z | x)/E_x' P(Z | x')), and using automatic differentiation to propagate gradients to the neural network. To constrain MI(X; Z) to the value rho, lambda is tuned by dual gradient descent by applying its gradient (rho - MI(Z; X)), which incurs negligible additional cost as it is already computed for the neural network objective.

content.title: Reply
content.comment:
Dear authors,

I would first like to thank you for addressing my questions in the rebuttal, I had no further comments on them.

I have updated my score after the discussion between you and the other reviewers from “good paper, accept” to “marginally above the acceptance threshold”. In the following I give the reasoning behind this revision.

First of all, as I already stated before, the confidence in my initial score was low. I have only little background in information bottlenecks in machine learning. After closely following the discussion with the other reviewers, I am even less confident of my initial rating.

Notably, I stand by my judgement that the bound you propose is interesting and nicely embedded in its context. It is aligned with intuition and improves previous work, resolving some contradictions in the literature.

However, after the discussions and carefully rereading your updated draft, I have some concerns. The discussion on the bound being possibly vacuous due to infinite mutual information in some settings was not obvious to me. In the discussion you have agreed that indeed, this is a concern for a specific set of networks and in your updated draft you claim to have resolved this issue.

You classify all possible networks into {discrete/continuous} input domains and {stochastic/deterministic} neural networks. Agreement exists on the fact that discrete inputs and deterministic models produce finite MI, and therefore the bound applies in this case which interesting in itself.

For the other classes there has been some controversy upon whether the bound can also be applied to those. From what I understand, in your updated draft you state two ways to transform predictors and their inputs such that the bounds for a different class can be used where the MI is finite. The first is binning to obtain a new predictor that is sufficiently similar but then has finite MI: Here the there is a concern that the Lipschitz constant of the loss that is then entering the bound might be very large. This would influence the meaningfulness of the bounds, and is thus a bit questionable, although binning is apparently done a lot in practice. The second is a general idea that moving from predictors with possibly infinite MI to predictors with finite MI for a generalization bound is possible, as long as the distance in loss between the two predictors is not too large whp.
The question here is again, whether finding such a close predictor is possible and if its MI means something for the original predictor. You conclude that these transformations can take you back to the class of networks you proved it for, so it holds (non-vacuously) for all NN.

Overall, you dedicate a good portion of the core theory part of the revised paper to showing these transformations. The bound is presented and then the applicability to infinite MI is discussed and extended as much as possible theoretically, although with arguments that, as I have explained above, are not always entirely conclusive.

To me, these infinite MI arguments seem like they should belong rather to the discussion of your experiments, where due to the difficulty of measuring the MI in real applications you actually have to resort to approximations of this value for given predictors. I would suggest that this context seems more appropriate for a discussion on the infinite MI, rather than the theoretical derivation for the specific network and input type you prove.

Finally, I do understand that these controversies about measuring the MI have been around  in the field for a while, which ofc should not prevent anyone from doing research on this. It took me some time reading your draft to figure out how to interpret your results in its context, which admittedly might simply be due to my non-matching background and not to the typical audience of your paper.
However, I still think the manuscript would benefit greatly if those considerations were contextualized correctly and I encourage you to keep working on it.
Given this line of thought, I now give the paper a score of “marginally above the acceptance threshold”.

I hope you find some of my feedback useful for the next iteration.
Best,

We believe that this improved the paper a lot, thanks to your feedback. Overall, the revision refined the main text and also increased the length of the paper from 37 pages to 47 pages with new experimental results and explanations. Below we respond to each of your comments.

---
---

**Reviewer’s Comment**: “the technical details are hard to read, especially with their notations that I find their separation of notations between random variables and their realizations make it complicated and unncessary.” 

**Response**: We made a series of revisions to make the technical details easier to read:

(2) We extensively revised the main text to focus on the main theoretical results for better clarity by moving propositions and extra definitions to appendix. As a result, we could remove a lot of complicated notation in the main text where we now explain our bounds and proofs with much simpler notation only. This improved the readability and clarity of the paper a lot. 
  
(3) We added a new appendix, Appendix B.1, for an overview of the proofs. Moreover, we changed the structure of the proof sections in order to make the proofs clearer in appendix B.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes an improvement over a complexity bound on Neural Networks based on Information Bottleneck theory by Schwartz-Ziv et al. (2019). In particular, the previously proposed version of a bound is not valid for a trainable representation, which is the case for the models of interest. Authors derive a novel bound that replaces the exponential term in the older bound with I(X;Z|Y). The main result is a bound for the trainable representation, that includes also the mutual information between dataset and neural network parameters. The authors verify the obtained complexity bounds via evaluating the correlation between generalization gap and the derived mutual information terms.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper investigates an extremely interesting approach to the generalization bounds of deep learning models. While the previous attempts are proven to fail for particular cases this represents an open area of research.

The authors put significant effort into formally proving the bounds based on information-theoretic quantities.

My main concern is with the infamous contraversy of measuring I(X;Z) for a deterministic neural network. As it was proven in Amjad et al. (2019) the true value of such mutual information is infinite for continuous distributions and deterministic networks. In the paper it is clearly stated in the discussion of the constants of the bound that the constants become O(1) (which is required for further use of the bound) only in the case of deterministic networks. In such case all the correlation empirical results observed are arbitrary and depend on the way MI was evaluated.
Another weakness of the paper is absence of the proof sketches in the main paper text. While it includes discussion on the benefits of the selected approach to the bound, it will be much more useful to provide the idea of the proof to ease the possibility to verify correctness of the theory for a reader.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper can be nicely followed, but the proof sketches will significantly improve the quality of the main text of the paper.
Also, some discussions after Theorem2 are not so clearly formulated. Paragraph4 on page 6 discusses why other information theoretic bounds are different from the proposed one. In particular the argument is that I(f; S) is different from I(X;Z|Y). But as explained later it is the same as I(\phi; S) that is also used in the bound. Moreover, what does it mean that for the last layer one term is nullified? That other information-theoretic bounds consider only singleton models? Paragraph5 claims that SGD and dropout are deterministic as long as the seed is fixed. While it is true for practical reasons it cannot be taken as a reason to claim in the theoretical analysis that a model is deterministic in such cases. This line of discussion is completely unclear to me.
It is unclear to me why the first experiment is performed on a Bayesian neural network without explicitly stating it. Moreover, having a toy example with possibility to sample any amount of data, one would expect a better correlation of generalization gap with the proposed values, since they can be computed more precisely (through Monte-Carlo). Nevertheless, the observed correlation on a toy example is 0.28, while for CIFAR10 and ResNet it is 0.86. It hints that more precise calculation of the values leads to worse results? Moreover, Fig.1 includes networks with negative generalization gap, i.e., undertrained networks. 
In the explanation of the SWAG usage for experiment1 (paragraph 2, section 4.1) some "scalings" are mentioned that are normalized by I(X;Z|Y). Why there is a need for scaling when mutual information is measured in universal units? Moreover, for computing mutual information of dataset with parameters, one also needs samples of datasets. How exactly is it implemented?

Up to my knowledge the work is novel.

The paper includes code for running the experiments, thus reproducibility is possible.

Typos:
- it should be $G^l_3$ in equation(14)
- in Theorem2 $G_4^l$ is mentioned before using
- Theorem 2 on page 6, paragraph 2
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper analyses the generalization bounds based on information-theoretic properties of deep neural networks. New perspective is proposed, that includes conditional (on label) mutual information and mutual information between data and parameters. The correlation of these key values with generalization gap is empirically evaluated.
Overall, the critical part is the consideration of deterministic neural networks with continuous distributions, which results in bounding generalization gap with infinity. Based on this, no matter of the theoretically grounded results, the resulting bounds might be completely not applicable and performed experiments not reflecting the true mutual information values.

content.title: Response to Reviewer iWuz (1/4)
content.comment:
Thank you for the feedback and positive comments that “the paper investigates an extremely interesting approach to the generalization bounds of deep learning models” and “the paper can be nicely followed”.  

We extensively revised the paper and resolved all of your concerns by adding new sections and new theoretical and experimental results in both main text and appendix. Overall, these revisions refined the main text and also increased the length of the paper from 37 pages to 47 pages. Thanks to your comments, we believe this improved the paper a lot. Below we respond to each of your comments.

---------
---------

**Reviewer’s Comment**: “My main concern is with the infamous contraversy of measuring I(X;Z) for a deterministic neural network. As it was proven in Amjad et al. (2019) the true value of such mutual information is infinite for continuous distributions and deterministic networks. In the paper it is clearly stated in the discussion of the constants of the bound that the constants become O(1) (which is required for further use of the bound) only in the case of deterministic networks.” and “Overall, the critical part is the consideration of deterministic neural networks with continuous distributions, which results in bounding generalization gap with infinity. Based on this, no matter of the theoretically grounded results, the resulting bounds might be completely not applicable”.

**Response**: We completely resolved the main concern of this reviewer through the following series of revisions. We cited the results of Amjad et al. (2019) and added new results and explanations to clearly show why these issues do not provide any concerns for our results as follows. First, the following revisions clarify that (1) the mutual information is not always infinite even for the case of deterministic neural networks with continuous distributions (for example, with ReLU), and (2) even when the mutual information is infinite, it does not provide any concern for our results because a trivial application of Theorems 1–2 always provides finite bounds with a finite version of mutual information that is used in practice:

- (1) We added a new proposition at the end of Section 3.2, stating the following: if we use ReLU activations, then there are infinitely many continuous distributions over the input space such that there are deterministic neural networks with finite mutual information I(X,Z|Y). That is, the reviewer’s statement, “As it was proven in Amjad et al. (2019) the true value of such mutual information is infinite for continuous distributions and deterministic networks”, is inaccurate and disproven in this new proposition. Instead, what Amjad et al. (2019) proved is that the true value of such mutual information is infinite for continuous distributions and deterministic networks, *when we use a special type of activation functions, which does not include ReLU*. Thus, with ReLU activations, the mutual information can be finite. 

- (2) For the case with infinite mutual information, we added 3 new results and 2 new sections, Corollary 1, Remark 2, Proposition 4, Section 3.3, and Appendix A.2. Through these new results, we explain why and how our theorems, Theorems 1-2, provide meaningful *finite* bounds even for the case with infinite mutual information. For example, Corollary 1 shows that even when the mutual information of the original model is infinite, Theorems 1–2 always provide finite generalization bounds on the same original model (without modifying the model) using the finite mutual information returned by a binning method on the original model. In other words, instead of using the *true* mutual information of the given model, which can be infinite, our bounds (on the same given model) can use a mutual information returned by a binning method, which is always finite. This is mathematically proven to be theoretically valid. A similar fact holds for other methods of computing mutual information including those of injecting noise and kernel density estimation, which was used by experiments in section 4.2 (note that the experiments on clustering, MNIST and Fashion MNIST use stochastic feature networks). Please see Section 3.3 and Appendix A.2 for more details. 

- (3) We did not include this technique of dealing with infinite mutual information in the submission because this is a trivial consequence of combining our results and a known trick in the circle of experts when we apply a bound or a method for the case of infinite mutual information: for example, see (Chelombiev et al., 2019) for a method, and see Corollary 3 of (Xu & Raginsky, 2017) for a bound. However, we agree that it is better to explicitly and formally mention this technique for a wider audience. Thanks to your comment, we were able to improve the paper a lot by explicitly including this.

content.title: Response to Reviewer iWuz (2/4)
content.comment:
Second, although the reviewer narrows the scope of our paper to deterministic networks for continuous distributions, we clarify that our results are also useful for stochastic networks with both continuous and discrete distributions, and for deterministic networks with discrete distributions:

- (1) At the beginning of Section 3.3, we added the following explanations. The mutual information for the information bottleneck is finite for many practical cases including the cases of discrete domains with any models and of continuous domains with stochastic models. For example, the mutual information is finite for deterministic networks with discrete domains. 

- (2) Even when the networks are stochastic, we typically have $H(Z_{l}^s|X,Y) = O(1)$. For example, consider an encoder of the form $Z_{l}^s = \phi_l^s(X) + A$ where $\phi_l^s$ is deterministic and $A$ is a noise term that we can choose. Then, $H(Z_{l}^s|X,Y) = H(A) = O(1)$, by choosing the noise term $A$ such that $H(A)=O(1)$

- (3) Our theoretical results are applicable for all of 4 cases, including 1) stochastic networks for continuous distributions, 2) stochastic networks for discrete distributions, 3) deterministic networks for continuous distributions, and 4) deterministic networks for discrete distributions. The reviewer only focused on the third case. Even for the third case, our bounds are useful as discussed above. 

- (4) Experimental results in sec 4.1 and appendix D use stochastic feature networks instead of deterministic networks. This is not a Bayesian neural network as explained below. The experimental results in sec 4.2 use the deterministic networks. The KDE estimator of mutual information for the deterministic networks in sec 4.2 directly follows the previous paper (Chelombiev et al. ICLR 2019).

Finally, we explain below that the relation between “the infamous controversy of measuring I(X;Z) for a deterministic neural network” and our paper has been misconceived by the reviewer and that the controversy does not apply for our paper:

- (1) The controversy is on the topic of **directly** using the true mutual information for deterministic networks **during the training process of neural networks, not at the stage of generalization evaluation**. If we directly use it, it can be infinite or piecewise constant, both of which are not good as a training objective. This is similar to the issue of directly using 0-1 loss during the training: we need some surrogate function of 0-1 loss. The same logic works for mutual information. For example, being piecewise constant is of no issue for generalization evaluation. Indeed, 0-1 loss is piecewise constant, and we cannot use it for training (with gradient-based optimizer) but we can use it for evaluation of the model. Similarly, piecewise constant mutual information is not an issue for the evaluation of the model although it can be an issue as a training objective. Similarly to the 0-1 loss, this suggests that we should use some surrogate function of mutual information for training, which has been explored in other works. Note that for our empirical experiments, we only optimize mutual information in section 4.1 and Appendix D, and the models for these experiments have stochastic latent features.

- (2) For the generalization evaluation, there are already well-established approaches to avoid this controversy: for example, see Corollary 3 of [1] for a theory and see [2] for a method. Indeed, more recently, the information bottleneck has been proven useful in practice despite the controversy: e.g., see [3-4].

- (3) In the case where the mutual information of the original model is infinite, there is already an accepted solution; i.e., computing the mutual information of its surrogate model that is finite. Please see (Chelombiev et al., 2019) for example. Our new results in Section 3.3 and Appendix A.2 prove that this solution is indeed theoretically valid. Thus, the controversy does not apply here.

[1] Xu, A., & Raginsky, M. Information-theoretic analysis of generalization capability of learning algorithms. NeurIPS 2017.

[2] Chelombiev, I., Houghton, C., & O'Donnell, C. Adaptive estimators show information compression in deep neural networks. ICLR 2019.

[3] Federici, M., Dutta, A., Forré, P., Kushman, N., & Akata, Z. Learning Robust Representations via Multi-View Information Bottleneck. In International Conference on Learning Representations. ICLR 2020.

[4] Lee, K. H., Arnab, A., Guadarrama, S., Canny, J., & Fischer, I. Compressive visual representations. NeurIPS 2021.

content.title: Response to Reviewer iWuz (3/4)
content.comment:
**Reviewer’s Comment**: “the proof sketches will significantly improve the quality of the main text of the paper”.

**Response**: We revised the paper directly following your comment as follows:

(1) We added the proof sketch in the new section, Section 3.4, along with a new proof idea, improving the explanation of the proofs by conveying the intuitions. 

(2) We added a new appendix, Appendix B.1, for an overview of the proofs. Moreover, we changed the structure of the proof sections in order to make the proofs clearer in appendix B. 

---------
---------

**Reviewer’s comment**: “Also, some discussions after Theorem2 are not so clearly formulated. Paragraph4 on page 6 discusses why other information theoretic bounds are different from the proposed one. In particular the argument is that I(f; S) is different from I(X;Z|Y). But as explained later it is the same as I(\phi; S) that is also used in the bound”.

**Response**: We revised the paragraph after Theorem 2 by adding better and additional explanations and by adding a new appendix section, Appendix A.3 “On comparisons with previous information-theoretic bounds”. 

Please note that other information theoretic bounds do not utilize the information bottleneck $I(X;Z_{l}^s|Y)$ (or $I(X;Z_{l}^s)$) and only uses $I(f^{S}; S)$, the mutual information between the training dataset $S$ and the \textit{entire} model $f^{S}=\phi^S_{D+1}$. Thus, the previous bounds cannot provide insights or justifications on the information bottleneck principle unlike our bounds. Therefore, our bounds and other information theoretic bounds are very different. 

Moreover, in our experiments, we demonstrate the advantage of $I(X;Z_{l}^s|Y)+I(\phi_{l}^{S}; S)$ in our bound over $I(f^{S}; S)$ in other information theoretic bounds. 

Furthermore, notice that $I(\phi_{l}^{S}; S) \neq I(f^{S}; S)$ for any $l\neq D+1$, and $I(\phi_{1}^{S}; S)\le \cdots \le I(\phi_{D}^{S}; S) \le I(\phi_{D+1}^{S}; S) = I(f^{S}; S)$

----
----

**Reviewer’s Question**: Moreover, what does it mean that for the last layer one term is nullified? That other information-theoretic bounds consider only singleton models?

**Response**: Yes, other information-theoretic bounds only consider the setting where the hypothesis space of the decoder g is a singleton. In the previous bounds, since the hypothesis space of the decoder g is singleton, there is no need for the encoder to provide a bottleneck to control the complexity of the hypothesis space of the decoder. In contrast, we consider non-singleton hypothesis spaces of decoders and utilize the information bottleneck of the encoder to control the complexity of the decoder. This also illustrates the difficulty of proving our sample complexity bounds with the information bottleneck where we need to consider the non-singleton hypothesis space for the decoder. We added this explanation in Appendix A.3.

----
----

**Reviewer’s Comment**: “It is unclear to me why the first experiment is performed on a Bayesian neural network without explicitly stating it.” 

**Response**: Thank you, we have edited Section 4.1 to clarify this point. This is not a Bayesian neural network. The weights of the instantiated neural networks are deterministic, the learning algorithm producing the weights is in general stochastic, and the neural network infers a distribution over a stochastic features Z so that I(X; Z) can be regularized and evaluated directly during training. Stochastic features are often used for mutual information regularization, see e.g. Alemi et al. 2016 and Eysenbach et al. 2021. 

---
---

**Reviewer’s Comment**: “Moreover, having a toy example with possibility to sample any amount of data, one would expect a better correlation of generalization gap with the proposed values, since they can be computed more precisely (through Monte-Carlo). Nevertheless, the observed correlation on a toy example is 0.28, while for CIFAR10 and ResNet it is 0.86. It hints that more precise calculation of the values leads to worse results?” 

**Response**: Thank you, we re-conducted the experiments using the true data generator to estimate I(X; Z) with a larger number of samples, and found that it does improve predictive performance of the metrics. We revised Section 4.1 and appendix C to incorporate the updated numbers and discussed this specifically in C.3. The main message is unchanged as incorporating model compression still improves prediction of the generalization gap. 

----
----

[Continued in the next post...]

content.title: Response to Reviewer iWuz (4/4)
content.comment:
**Reviewer’s Comment**: Paragraph 5 claims that SGD and dropout are deterministic as long as the seed is fixed. While it is true for practical reasons it cannot be taken as a reason to claim in the theoretical analysis that a model is deterministic in such cases. This line of discussion is completely unclear to me.

**Response**: We revised the corresponding parts for better presentation. We added the following in the appendix A.1.2. To understand this, let us consider a real-world experiment with a coin tossing. We can model the coin tossing by a stochastic model (by saying that coin tossing has 50-50 chance of getting heads and tails) or by a deterministic model to predict the exact outcome with an exact initial condition of the physical system. Similarly, we can model a single real-world algorithm with a stochastic model $A_l$ (by saying that something has some random chances) or a deterministic model $A_l$ with the exact initial condition, which is the random seed in the numerical experiments. That is, as in any mathematical theories and symbols, $A_l$ is a theoretical placeholder with its mathematical definition; i.e., $A_l$ does not have one-to-one correspondence to a real-world algorithm implemented in experiments. In other words, given a single real-world algorithm, there are many different ways to model the real-world algorithm and different ways result in different $A_l$. For example, let us fix the real-world algorithm implemented in experiments to be one with dropout and stochastic gradient descent (SGD). At this point, $A_l$ in Theorem 2 is not fully determined yet and we can choose $A_l$ differently for the same real-world algorithm by modeling the real-world differently. For instance, we can model the one with dropout and SGD as a stochastic algorithm or as a deterministic algorithm given a fixed random seed in practice. Thus, we can set $A_l$ in Theorem 2 to be either a stochastic algorithm or a deterministic algorithm for the exact same real-world and the same fixed algorithm implemented in experiments. If we set $A_l$ to be a deterministic algorithm with a fixed seed, then we have $H_{}(\phi_{l}^S|S)=0$. If we set $A_l$ to be a stochastic algorithm, then we increase $H(\phi_{l}^S|S)$ but we can potentially decrease $I(\phi_{l}^{S}; S)$ since the extra randomness can potentially reduce the mutual information of $\phi_{l}^{S}$ and $S$. Thus, there is a trade-off in how we model the real-world via $A_l$ and we cannot reduce the bound arbitrarily. Our theorems allow to instantiate our bounds with both deterministic and stochastic views of the learning algorithms, without changing the real-world algorithms.

---
---

**Reviewer’s Comment**: “Moreover, Fig.1 includes networks with negative generalization gap, i.e., undertrained networks.” 

**Response**: Indeed, a small number of models in this section (9, or 5%) attained a negative generalization gap. The gap is not measurable without access to labelled test data, which is why we did not remove these models when computing results. We have added a part clarifying this in C.1. There were no negative generalization gaps observed for the other 3 datasets.

---
---

**Reviewer’s Comment**: “In the explanation of the SWAG usage for experiment1 (paragraph 2, section 4.1) some "scalings" are mentioned that are normalized by I(X;Z|Y). Why there is a need for scaling when mutual information is measured in universal units? Moreover, for computing mutual information of dataset with parameters, one also needs samples of datasets. How exactly is it implemented?”

**Response**: We have added a part clarifying this point in C.2. MI is measured in universal units, but we test multiple estimation procedures for I(X; Z) and I(theta; S). Scaling was tested not because of difference in units of the estimated quantity but because of the difference in estimators.

To sample multiple datasets, the data generator was used for experiments in Section 4.1, and for CIFAR10 we sampled 5 15K-sized subsets of training set, which was stated in Section 4.2.


---
---

Finally, we fixed the typos according to your comments. Thank you!

content.title: More clarification
content.comment:
Thanks again for your answers.

I understand your explanation of why a stochastic experiment can be described as deterministic, but if I get it correctly, you claim that it is possible when we already know everything what happened (or have a deterministic way of generating random outcomes, i.e., like in python implementation with seeds). If it is your claim, I do not see why it allows to describe training of a stochastic neural network as deterministic process overall - if we try to apply a bound for any network obtained through the same stochastic process.

content.title: Author response
content.comment:
Thank you again for your questions. 

**Reviewer's Question**: I understand your explanation of why a stochastic experiment can be described as deterministic, but if I get it correctly, you claim that it is possible when we already know everything what happened (or have a deterministic way of generating random outcomes, i.e., like in python implementation with seeds). If it is your claim, I do not see why it allows to describe training of a stochastic neural network as deterministic process overall - if we try to apply a bound for any network obtained through the same stochastic process.

**Authors' Answer**: No, this is not what we are claiming. We revised the paper by adding the following explanation in Section A.1.2 to make it clearer:

- This is the mathematical and well-known fact beyond our paper: i.e., we can model these numerical experiments in both stochastic or deterministic ways.  That is, we are not making any new claim on this. Instead, this is simply a well-known fact. For example, [1] explains that "Another possibility is to consider a randomized algorithm as a deterministic algorithm with an additional input that consists of a sequence of random bits. In other words, a randomized algorithm may be seen as a set of deterministic algorithms, from which one algorithm is randomly chosen for the given input." Here, the sequence of random bits corresponds to the sequence of random seeds. In other words, on the one hand, we can model SGD as a stochastic process when we analyze **a set of experiments** with SGD over a set of random seeds that are generated randomly. On the other hand, we can model SGD as a deterministic process when we analyze **each experiment** with SGD for each random seed. Moreover, as [1] explains, we can bridge those 2 cases by modeling SGD as a deterministic algorithm with its additional inputs being the seed; then (1) it is deterministic for each seed, and (2) we can recover the stochastic model by considering a sequence of the randomly generated seeds. More generally, the sequence of random bits does not need to be corresponding to random seeds. Given any stochastic algorithm, the stochasticity of an algorithm can be formalized via measure theory, with a probability measure space. In other words, any stochastic algorithm is defined by a deterministic measurable function from a probability measure space to a measurable space. Here, the deterministic measurable function is the deterministic version of the algorithm. Thus, for each an input from the probability measure space, any stochastic algorithm is defined as a deterministic algorithm. To consider stochasticity, we vary the input from the probability measure space and consider how the behavior of the deterministic algorithm varies. This is the formal definition of stochasticity. 

- **Therefore, we can mathematically model SGD in both deterministic and stochastic ways **always**, not "when we already know everything what happened", contrary to your comment**. If we analyze **each experiment** of SGD for each random seed, then we have a deterministic algorithm, and a typical worst-case analysis provides a guarantee on the SGD with the worst seed. But, if we analyze **a set of experiments** of SGD over a set of random seeds that are generated randomly, then we have a stochastic algorithm, and we can analyze its expected performance or high-probability guarantee where the probability is with respect to the random seeds. Indeed, there is a whole subfield about this relationship of modeling the same algorithm stochastically and deterministically in the theory of randomized algorithms and "beyond worst-case analysis".   

I wish I could meet you in person to explain it more. Meanwhile, for the purpose of this paper, (1) this is the mathematical and well-known fact [1]-[2], and (2) this is not an important property that our paper depends on. Our results are not affected by this discussion since our results are valid for both cases of stochastic or deterministic modeling of SGD and numerical simulations. Thus, this point should not affect the review of our paper. 

We understand the confusion of the reviewer because understanding this point fully requires a good understanding of measure theory. We recommend reading [2] to understand this in more details. Being said that, we are happy to explain it more if there is still a question. Please let us know. 


[1] Hromkovič, J. (2004). Randomized Algorithms. In Algorithmics for Hard Problems (pp. 341-429). Springer, Berlin, Heidelberg.

[2] Ash, R. B., Robert, B., Doleans-Dade, C. A., & Catherine, A. (2000). Probability and measure theory. Academic press.

content.title: More clarification
content.comment:
I thank the authors for the thorough response and huge work done on the submission.

I want to clarify once again the statements made in the comments:
1 - You claim that there is no problem with discrete domain input, stochastic networks and ReLU networks.
2 - You claim that binning can give a (precise?) measurement of mutual information even in the case when true value is infinite. Or, as I shortly saw in your editions in the paper, you can balance somehow the measurement in the boundary?

I also want to add, that infinite mutual information is not a problem for training with information bottleneck obviously (though my guess that it still can very well lead to spurious results), but I am much more concerned with precision of the generalization bound when it is (mathematically) infinite. It might be that specifying point (1) is a good clarification for the applicability area of the bound, which is far from small in any way.

content.title: Author response
content.comment:
We thank Reviewer iWuz for noticing that "the applicability area of the bound is far from small". 

- We revised the paper by directly following your additional comment that "specifying point (1) is a good clarification for the applicability area of the bound, which is far from small in any way." We added this sentence of "there is no problem with discrete domain input, stochastic networks and ReLU networks" in the 1st paragraph of Section 3.3.

- You and we all agree now that our results are applicable in the area of "discrete domain input, stochastic networks, and ReLU networks", which is far from small. **This seems to resolve your concern for a purpose of reviewing a paper because a paper is expected to have some reasonable scope and the scope of "discrete domain input, stochastic networks, and ReLU networks" is already reasonable**. But, we also point out below that our results are applicable beyond this scope and when mutual information is infinite:

**Reviewer's Question**: You claim that binning can give a (precise?) measurement of mutual information even in the case when true value is infinite. Or, as I shortly saw in your editions in the paper, you can balance somehow the measurement in the boundary?

**Authors' Answer**: "Yes" for the 2nd question (i.e., "No" for the 1st question); we can balance the measurement in the boundary. That is, we mathematically proved that we can balance the measurement such that (1) binning always produces **the finite version** of the true mutual information even when the true mutual information is infinite, and (2) we can use **this finite version** of the true mutual information in our bounds to bound the generalization error of the original model without modifying the model. While this might look amazing, we should note that this is an immediate consequence of combining our bonds with a known technique of dealing with infinite mutual information at the stage of model evaluation: for example, see Corollary 3 of (Xu & Raginsky, 2017) for a bound and (Chelombiev et al., 2019) for a method. Accordingly, we added this new result as Corollary 1 of our theorems in the revised paper (instead of a new theorem).

We hope that these revisions and clarifications address your main concern, which is about infinite mutual information. Also, if you want to edit your comment based on our revisions and clarifications, we can edit (or remove) the direct quotation of your comments to anything you want if you want us to edit (or remove) it.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Drab (1/2)
content.comment:
Thank you for the review and commenting that “the paper presents new bounds, along with the proof” and “the paper presents the problem, along with the motivation to study the problem”.

We extensively revised the paper according to all of your comments by adding a new section of a proof sketch and new experimental results with more datasets and by revising papers for better clarity. Overall, these revisions refined the main text and also increased the length of the paper from 37 pages to 47 pages. We believe that this improved the paper a lot, thanks to your comments. Below we respond to each of your comments.

-----------------------------------------------------
-----------------------------------------------------


**Reviewer’s Comment**: “It will be interesting to see the results on additional datasets.” 

**Response**: Based on your comment, we added 2 more common datasets, Fashion MNIST and MNIST. The results for these experiments can be found in new Appendix D and are in line with conclusions from section 4: one can expect incorporating model compression metrics to improve the prediction of generalization gaps, demonstrating the significance of our new theoretical finding. The key new observations can be summarized as (see tables 7 & 8 for full results):

| MNIST | Spearman | Pearson | Kendall | 
| --- | --- | --- | --- | 
| Best representation compression metric | 0.7931 | 0.5467 | 0.6416 |
| Best model and representation compression metric | **0.8352** | **0.7626** |  **0.6452** |


| Fashion MNIST | Spearman | Pearson | Kendall | 
| --- | --- | --- | --- | 
| Best representation compression metric | 0.3861 | 0.5146 |  0.2308 | 
| Best model and representation compression metric | **0.5637** | **0.6488** | **0.4344** |

Here, "representation compression metric" and "model compression metric" correspond to $I(Z; X)$ and $I(\theta; S)$, respectively.

For your question on “why these datasets were chosen”, please note that for each dataset, we  varied architectures and other learning settings, originally testing 756 regimes in total. Thus, unlike common experimental setups, we cannot choose many datasets without increasing energy consumption a lot, which is not good for sustainability and unrealistic for limited computational resources. Under such a constraint, we chose the datasets (clustering and CIFAR10) to cover both a standard toy problem and a standard deep learning benchmark. However, given this comment, we added 2 additional datasets as reported above.

-----------------------------------------------------
-----------------------------------------------------

**Reviewer’s Comment**: “The proof for theorem 1, which is the primary aspect of the paper to show the bounds is not clearly explained. The authors have presented the proof in Appendix A and Appendix B. However, it is not clear how eq13 follows from the proofs, as currently presented in the paper.” 

**Response**: We made the following series of revisions for this comment:

(1) We revised the proof of Theorem 1 for a better clarity by adding the restatement of Lemma 6 and by adding the following extra explanations. Recall that we proved Lemma 6 in Appendix B.1 (originally Appendix A). The proof of Theorem 1 in Appendix B.2 (originally Appendix B) directly follows from Lemma 6. That is, Appendix B.2 completes the proof of Theorem 1 using Lemma 6 from Appendix B.1. Please see Appendix B.2. in the revised paper for more details. The proof of Theorem 1 is much clearer now with the restatement of Lemma 6, thanks to your comment.

(2) We added the new section, Section 3.4, for new proof sketches, improving the explanation of the proofs by conveying the intuitions. 

(3) We added a new appendix, Appendix B.1, for an overview of the proofs. Moreover, we changed the structure of the proof sections in order to make the proofs clearer in appendix B.  

(4) We extensively revised the main text to focus on the main theoretical results for better clarity (and for the page limit) by moving propositions and extra definitions to appendix. This improved the readability and clarity of the paper a lot. 

These revisions make it clearer on how the main results follow from the proofs. Finally, please notice that the full proofs in appendix are complete and our results follow directly from the proofs without any ambiguity in the sense of mathematical proofs. 


-----------------------------------------------------
-----------------------------------------------------

**Reviewer’s Question**: One minor question about eq 12 - is that a "=" or a bound (either <= or >=)?

**Response**: this is a bound with the equal sign, "=", as it uses the Big O notation. Very roughly speaking, you can think of this as a bound with <= sign if you wish. But technically, this should be an equal sign even though this is a bound. For example, please see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_O_notation.

--------------
---------------

content.title: Response to Reviewer Drab (2/2)
content.comment:
**Reviewer’s Comment**: “In this paper, the authors present an analysis of information bottlenecks, and present an improved bound for the the gap between the expected loss and the training loss. They bound has a linear growth rate compared to the previous bound by Shwartz-Ziv et al. The authors present extensive proofs and analysis of their improved bounds.”

**Response**: We revised the paper to avoid possible misunderstandings of our main contribution.

- This reviewer seems to miss our main contribution. Our main contribution is not the improvement of the previous bound. The improvement is just a by-product of our true main contribution. The true main contribution is the first information bottleneck bound on the setting of learning encoders. There is no previous bound on this setting. Instead of an improvement, we prove the first bound of this type in the literature, solving an open problem. Similarly, our main contribution is Theorem 2 instead of Theorem 1. 

- The importance and novelty of this is significantly different than an improvement. Thus, we hope that the reviewer can re-evaluate our paper by taking into account our true main contribution. For example, this point was clearly mentioned and evaluated in the reviews by Reviewer r4UJ. 

- However, we could be clearer on this point. Thus, we revised the introduction to make it clearer. For example, we now have the following sentences:

(1) In this paper, we resolve this open question by providing novel and complete proofs for end-to-end learning of intermediate representations (Theorem 2) where the previous bound does not work. As a byproduct of our novel proofs, we also improve the previous bound significantly in the setting of the previous works with a fixed random variable $Z$ (Theorem 1). 

(2) Our main result (Theorem 2) shows that for end-to-end learning of intermediate representations, the gap between the expected loss and the training loss scales roughly (with high probability) as […].
